title: A Ledger for the Parish
premise: Estate lawyer Ines Underhill is summoned to the coastal parish of Marrow Bay to read the will of Aldous Vane, its founder, who died forty years ago. The will, dated three days after his burial, leaves everything to a woman no one can find—and when the parish council insists on exhuming Vane to settle a land dispute, his coffin proves empty. Ines traces the will to Vane's secretary, Miriam Hale, who faked his death to help him escape a life he no longer wanted; the two lived out their days in a house above the tideline that now sits inside the disputed parcel. To close the case, Ines must prove Vane was alive after his 'death' without destroying Miriam's posthumous reputation or the town's memory of its founder, and he ends by filing a quiet amended record: Aldous Vane died where he chose, with whom he chose, and the ledger finally balances.
about_author: S. M. Sterling spent a decade as a probate clerk in small coastal towns before turning to fiction, and still keeps a drawer of wills that were never filed. A Ledger for the Parish is their third novel and first mystery.

chapters.title: The Reading
chapters.summary: Ines Underhill arrives in rain-soaked Marrow Bay to read the will of Aldous Vane, dead forty years, at the request of an anonymous client fee paid in old banknotes. The document is dated after the burial and names a beneficiary: M. Hale. POV: Ines. Beat: professional curiosity curdling into unease.

chapters.title: A Town That Remembers Wrongly
chapters.summary: Ines interviews the parish council, who treat Vane's founding as gospel and the will as forgery. The church sexton mentions the grave has never been opened. POV: Ines. Beat: the town's polished memory feels rehearsed, like a story everyone agreed to tell.

chapters.title: M. Hale
chapters.summary: Research reveals Miriam Hale, Vane's secretary, who left Marrow Bay the same month he died and never returned. Her descendants are untraceable. POV: Ines. Beat: the first thread pulled; Ines notes he never takes a case he can't close.

chapters.title: The Dispute
chapters.summary: Developer Corliss Vance claims the tideland parcel under the old Hale property, forcing the council to demand physical proof Vane is buried there. An exhumation order is signed. POV: Ines. Beat: dread—the case is about to become public.

chapters.title: What the Tide Keeps
chapters.summary: The exhumation draws half the town. The coffin, lowered with full honors in 1984, is empty except for river stones arranged in a deliberate pattern. POV: alternating Ines and elderly witness Edith Crane. Beat: communal shock; Edith weeps for reasons she won't name.

chapters.title: Stones from the Shoreline
chapters.summary: Ines identifies the stones as coming from the beach below the abandoned Hale house—miles from any quarry. Someone carried them there before the funeral. POV: Ines. Beat: cold clarity; this was planned by people who loved him.

chapters.title: Edith's Silence
chapters.summary: Ines presses Edith Crane, Vane's housekeeper, who admits she helped dress the coffin but swears she believed Vane lay inside until the lid closed. She gives him a key taped under a hymnal. POV: Edith. Beat: guilt and loyalty at war.

chapters.title: The House Above the Tideline
chapters.summary: Inside the sealed Hale house, Ines finds two toothbrushes, decades of grocery ledgers in two hands, and a photograph of Vane and Miriam laughing on the porch, dated 1991. POV: Ines. Beat: wonder—he was alive here, all along, twenty feet from the town's memory.

chapters.title: Corliss Moves
chapters.summary: Vance learns of the empty coffin and threatens to expose the fraud unless the parish concedes the land, which would demolish the house. The council turns on Ines. POV: Ines. Beat: pressure mounting; his invisibility strategy collapses.

chapters.title: The Second Will
chapters.summary: In a locked desk, Ines finds a second document: Vane's true account, written in his own hand, confessing he staged his death to flee debts and a marriage that had become a cage, with Miriam's help. It asks only to be left in peace. POV: Ines reading aloud, alone. Beat: tenderness for the dead.

chapters.title: A Marriage in the Ledger
chapters.summary: Records show Vane's wife, Eleanor, inherited everything in 1984 and quietly funded the parish ever since—hush money, perhaps, or penance. Eleanor's nephew confirms she knew and chose silence. POV: Ines. Beat: love against duty refracted through Eleanor's choice.

chapters.title: Someone Else Is Reading
chapters.summary: The Hale house is searched overnight; the confession is missing. Footprints lead to the tideline and stop. POV: Ines. Beat: violation and fear—the truth is now a weapon someone else holds.

chapters.title: Corliss's Claim
chapters.summary: Vance presents the stolen confession to the council, demanding the land as the price of silence. Ines realizes Vance is Eleanor's estranged grandson, owed nothing by the real will. POV: Ines. Beat: the antagonist's motive snaps into focus: inheritance denied.

chapters.title: Edith Breaks
chapters.summary: Confronted with the theft, Edith confesses the whole scheme to the town at a parish meeting: how she sewed the stones into the shroud, how Miriam begged her forgiveness yearly by letter. POV: Edith. Beat: catharsis; the town's grief and fury collide.

chapters.title: The Town Decides
chapters.summary: Marlow Bay splits: some want Vane's statue toppled, others argue a man who gave them forty good years deserves his chosen ending. The vote on the exhumation fraud hangs on Ines's testimony. POV: Ines. Beat: the invisible man made visible, against his nature.

chapters.title: What Ines Won't Say
chapters.summary: On the stand-equivalent hearing, Ines testifies to documents but refuses to read the confession's intimate passages aloud, arguing the dead keep their private ledgers. Vance's lawyer pivots to attack Miriam's character instead. POV: Ines. Beat: duty bending toward mercy.

chapters.title: Miriam's Letters
chapters.summary: Ines locates Miriam's surviving granddaughter, Ruth, who possesses letters proving Vane's debts were repaid in full before his death—meaning the fraud harmed no heir but Vance, whose claim was already void. POV: Ruth. Beat: hope; the law may yet side with love.

chapters.title: The Storm
chapters.summary: A storm surge floods the tideline parcel, collapsing part of the bluff and exposing a buried strongbox on the Hale property containing Vane's original deathbed letter to the town, written in 2003. POV: Ines. Beat: the tide literally giving up what it took.

chapters.title: The Letter
chapters.summary: Read publicly, Vane's letter asks forgiveness, explains his flight, and deeds the tideland parcel to the parish outright—voiding Vance's claim forever. The town goes quiet, then begins, slowly, to forgive. POV: Ines. Beat: climax resolved not by exposure but by the man's own voice.

chapters.title: Corliss's Last Motion
chapters.summary: Vance files one final challenge; Ines dismantles it with the debt records and the deed, then offers him something unexpected: Eleanor's private letters showing she grieved him too. He withdraws. POV: Ines. Beat: mercy extended even to the adversary.

chapters.title: Amendments
chapters.summary: Ines files the amended record: Vane's true date and place of death, Miriam named as his partner, the fraud acknowledged and pardoned by parish resolution. Edith is laid to rest beside the stone-filled coffin she filled. POV: Ines. Beat: grief braided with peace.

chapters.title: Closing the Ledger
chapters.summary: Ines visits the Hale house one last time before it becomes a parish archive, leaves the two grocery ledgers open on the kitchen table, and walks the shoreline where the stones came from. He takes a new case—a living client—at last. POV: Ines. Beat: resolution; the man who stayed invisible learned what memory is for.
